newsitem.title: UK: Major, unbowed by polls, sees British election win.
newsitem.headline: Major, unbowed by polls, sees British election win.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, unbowed by opinion polls which appear to spell doom for his Conservatives, on Friday expressed continued confidence that they could win the upcoming British election.

Speaking on a day when two polls showed his party more than 20 points adrift of the opposition Labour Party, Major said: "Ours is a positive programme on which we'll fight and win the next general election."
"The new ideas are ours, the new plans are ours, the new agenda is ours," Major added in a speech to his constituency party in Huntingdon, eastern England.
Major is widely expected to call an election for May 1. But a poll in the Daily Telegraph, the bible for his party supporters, made many of them blanch when it landed on their breakfast tables.
It showed the gap between the Conservatives and Labour had widened to 26 points from 15 over the past month. Another poll in the Independent newspaper put the gap at 21 points.
However, Major said a radical Conservative plan to revamp Britain's pensions system announced this week showed that despite 18 years in office, the party had not run out of ideas.
"Our plans for pensions are the most far-reaching and farsighted that any government has unveiled for decades," he said.

Under the plans, young Britons would be freed from part of their traditional national insurance contributions provided they invested the money in a commercial pension plan, which Major says would offer them the possibility of much higher pensions.

He named plans to privatise London's underground railway, and to extend share ownership as further proof his party was still thinking radically, and pledged further policy announcements in the run-up to the election.
Major's optimism was despite headlines in British newspapers suggesting another controversy over food safety had set off feuding among his cabinet ministers.

The row concerned a report which pinpointed unhygienic conditions in abattoirs that could have spread disease to meat supplies. In Scotland, 20 people have been killed by an E.coli food poisoning outbreak.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth launched into a damage limitation exercise after reports that he was "incandescent" with rage over Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's handling of the report.
Forsyth, whose office on Thursday night issued a statement to say it had never seen the crucial food poisoning report, insisted there was no cabinet split.

"What I am angry about is the suggestion that there is a rift between Douglas Hogg and I on handling of the issue and I am angry about the suggestion that ministers knew about this report and somewhow sought to suppress it," he told BBC Radio.
But Labour was scornful with their Scottish spokesman George Robertson claiming: "The people who are supposed to be running the country don't know what is going on."
Hogg, already under fire over his handling of the mad cow crisis, denied in parliament he had suppressed the report.

Professor Hugh Pennington, the scientist appointed by the government to look into the E.coli outbreak, said he had not been told about the report and that it could have helped him in his investigation.
